intro: A hymn more than 3,000 years old asks how the world began and ends by wondering whether even its overseer knows. Another hymn in the same book describes a cosmic person and four classes of society. A queen asks a question no elder can answer. A warrior keeps faith with a friend against his own brothers. A queen passes through fire, and later returns to the earth.

In this unit you will read Rig Veda 10.129 and 10.90 closely in Griffith's translation (1896), and study four hard cases from the Mahabharata and the Ramayana. You will see how later traditions used the Purusha hymn, how reformers and scholars answered, and how devotees, feminist readers and poets such as Chandrabati have read the epics' hardest scenes.

By the end you will be able to cite a hymn or episode exactly, explain the dilemma it presents, and describe the range of Hindu and scholarly responses fairly, without treating any one reading as the verdict on Hindus or on the texts.
bigQuestion: How do ancient hymns and epic dilemmas pose hard questions, and how have different readers answered them?

test.q: How does Rig Veda 10.129 begin in Griffith's translation?
choices: Then was not non-existent nor existent
test.why: Griffith's first line of the Nasadiya Sukta.

test.q: How does the Hymn of Creation end?
choices: He verily knows it, or perhaps he knows not

test.q: What is born from Purusha's mind in 10.90?
test.why: The moon from his mind, the sun from his eye.

test.q: What is special about Rig Veda 10.90.12?
choices: It is the first verse of the Rig Veda
It is the only Rig Vedic verse naming all four varnas
test.why: Only 10.90.12 lists all four varnas together.

test.q: Who argued in 1946 that the Purusha verse was used to justify injustice?
test.why: Ambedkar's Who Were the Shudras? appeared in 1946.

test.q: Which reformer argued varna should follow merit, not birth?
test.why: The Arya Samaj founder took this position.

test.q: Why can the gods not tell how the world began, according to 10.129.6?
choices: They came later than the creation
test.why: Verse 6 says the gods are later than the world's creation.

test.q: What does Draupadi ask the assembly?
choices: Whether a man who lost himself could stake her
Why the Yaksha guards the lake
test.why: Her question turns on the order of the stakes.
Shakuni, a master of dice, threw for Duryodhana.

test.q: What does Yudhishthira call the greatest wonder?
choices: People see others die yet wish to live forever
The mind is faster than the wind
A mother is heavier than the earth
test.why: That is his answer to the Yaksha's most famous question.

test.q: Why does Yudhishthira choose Nakula to be revived?
choices: So each of Pandu's wives has a living son
test.why: His choice shows fairness between Kunti and Madri.

test.q: What promise does Karna make to Kunti?
choices: He will fight for the Pandavas
He will kill none of her sons but Arjuna
test.why: She will still have five sons either way.

test.q: Who returns Sita from the fire unharmed?
test.why: Agni, the fire god, rises and declares her pure.

test.q: What do many scholars think about the Uttara Kanda?
choices: It was added later than the epic's core
It is the oldest part of the Ramayana
It is part of the Rig Veda
test.why: Many scholars see it as later; many Hindus accept it as Valmiki's.

test.q: What did India's Constitution do in 1950?

write.prompt: Do the texts in this unit give clear answers to hard questions, or do they leave the questions open? Cite two or three passages (for example Rig Veda 10.129.7 in Griffith, Draupadi's question in the Sabha Parva, Sita's return in the Uttara Kanda), explain what each says, and describe how different readers have responded.
tips: Cite the text, book and verse or episode, and the translation.
Attribute every reading: devotees, reformers, scholars, poets.
Describe hard passages historically, never as a verdict on Hindus.
Compare readings; do not rank them.
Use the unit's terms: varna, sukshma, agni pariksha, dilemma.
